item.title: Aichi Events 2026: Nagoya Sumo, Fireworks, Tenno Festival & Ghibli Park
item.description: Aichi — with Nagoya at its heart — is the manufacturing engine of Japan, but its 2026 event calendar is pure summer spectacle and samurai heritage. The prefecture hosts a July Grand Sumo tournament in a brand-new arena, some of the country’s biggest fireworks in its “Mikawa fireworks” heartland, a 600-year-old UNESCO river festival, a procession of the three warlords who unified Japan, and Studio Ghibli’s own theme park. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Fukuoka Events 2026: Yamakasa, Dontaku, Kanmon Fireworks & Kyushu Sumo
item.description: Fukuoka wears its festival culture on its sleeve. Hakata — the old merchant heart of the city — hosts two of Kyushu’s most explosive festivals within months of each other (Dontaku in May, Yamakasa in July), the region’s only Grand Sumo tournament arrives each November, and one of Japan’s biggest fireworks displays lights up the Kanmon Strait in August. Add a week-long autumn shrine festival famous for its food stalls, and Fukuoka’s 2026 calendar rewards a well-timed trip.

item.title: Kanagawa Events 2026: Yokohama Fireworks, Tanabata & Hakone Parade
item.description: Kanagawa packs an unusual variety into one prefecture: the harbour glamour of Yokohama, the temples and beaches of Kamakura and Shonan, and the mountain onsen of Hakone. Its 2026 event calendar is just as varied — near-monthly fireworks over Yokohama’s port, one of the Kanto region’s three great Tanabata festivals, a feudal-lord procession through Hakone, and horseback archery at Kamakura’s great shrine. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Tokyo Events 2026: Festivals, Fireworks & One-Off Happenings
item.description: Tokyo runs on a calendar of its own. In any given month, the city is hosting a centuries-old shrine festival, a national sumo tournament, a fireworks display drawing a million spectators, a pop-culture collaboration that exists only in 2026, and a seasonal spectacle timed to the blossoms or the autumn leaves. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around — the fixed annual traditions, the summer fireworks, and the one-off happenings you can only catch this year — with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Kanmon Strait Fireworks Festival, Shimonoseki — Guide
item.description: The Kanmon Strait Fireworks Festival is one of the largest and most spectacular fireworks displays in western Japan, held each summer over the narrow strait between Shimonoseki and Kitakyushu in Kyushu. What makes it special is that both cities launch simultaneously from opposite shores, sending tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water in a friendly cross-strait rivalry, their light doubled by reflection on the sea and framed by the great Kanmon Bridge.

item.title: Matsuyama Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: The Matsuyama Summer Festival (Matsuyama Matsuri) is the city’s largest annual celebration, held over three evenings in mid-August. Its highlight is the ‘Yasakoi’ dance — teams of costumed dancers parade through the central streets performing an energetic, rhythmic routine, with a distinctive local flavour that has absorbed influences from samba and other styles into a joyful summer spectacle. Alongside the dancing, the festival brings food stalls, music and a buzzing street atmosphere to central Matsuyama, and is often rounded off with a fireworks display over the city.

item.title: Miyazaki Fireworks Festival — Guide
item.description: Summer in Miyazaki brings spectacular fireworks festivals (hanabi taikai), a beloved highlight of the Japanese summer. Miyazaki city’s display is among the largest in the region, launching thousands of fireworks over the river or coast on a warm evening and filling the night sky with brilliant bursts of colour, cascading golden willows, huge starbursts and creative choreographed sequences building to a thunderous grand finale. Held as part of the city’s summer festivities, the event draws big crowds who gather along the riverbanks, parks and viewing areas in the balmy night air, enjoying food stalls, festival treats and the electric atmosphere as they wait for the show.

item.title: Nagasaki Port Festival — Guide
item.description: The Nagasaki Port (Minato) Festival is a cheerful summer event celebrating the harbour that has always been the heart of the city’s life and history. Held on the waterfront, it brings the port area alive with a festive, communal atmosphere: rows of food and drink stalls, stages with music and performances, family activities and crowds strolling the harbourside on warm summer evenings. The highlight is a spectacular fireworks display launched over the water, the bursts reflected in the harbour and framed by the surrounding hills — a classic Japanese summer scene.

item.title: Oita Fireworks Festival — Guide
item.description: Summer in Oita brings spectacular fireworks festivals (hanabi taikai), a beloved centrepiece of the Japanese summer, and Oita city’s display is among the region’s biggest. On a warm evening, thousands of fireworks are launched over the river and city, filling the night sky with brilliant bursts of colour, cascading golden willows, huge starbursts and creative set-pieces choreographed to build to a thunderous finale, all reflected in the water below. Held as part of the city’s summer festivities, the event draws huge crowds who gather along the riverbanks and viewing areas in the warm night air, enjoying food stalls, festival treats and the electric atmosphere as they wait for the show.

item.title: Okayama Momotaro Festival: The City's Great Summer Party — Guide
item.description: The Momotaro Matsuri is Okayama city’s largest annual celebration, held over a weekend in early August and named for the Peach Boy legend rooted in the surrounding Kibi Plain. Its signature is the Uraja, a modern dance competition in which hundreds of teams parade through the streets in bold costumes with their faces painted in fierce patterns — a nod to Ura, the demon Momotaro is said to have defeated. Alongside it run mikoshi processions, taiko, hundreds of food stalls and, on the river, a large fireworks display that closes the weekend.

item.title: Takamatsu Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: The Takamatsu Festival (Takamatsu Matsuri) is the prefectural capital’s largest summer celebration, held over several days in mid-August. It fills the central streets and the harbour area with a lively mix of dance parades, music, performances, food and game stalls and a festive summer atmosphere, drawing crowds from across the region. Its grand finale is a spectacular fireworks display launched over Takamatsu’s harbour and the Seto Inland Sea, the bursts reflected in the calm water — one of the highlights of the Kagawa summer.

item.title: Tottori Shanshan Festival: Umbrella Dance and Summer — Guide
item.description: The Shanshan Festival is Tottori city’s biggest annual celebration, a vast summer street festival held in mid-August that fills the central streets with thousands of dancers. Its signature is the umbrella dance: performers twirl large, brightly decorated umbrellas hung with little bells, whose massed jingling gives the festival its onomatopoeic name, ‘shanshan’. The name also nods to the region’s hot springs, said to make you feel refreshed. By day and into the evening, waves of dancers in matching costumes fill the streets in one of Japan’s largest umbrella dances, and the festivities are rounded out with food stalls and, in the wider season, fireworks.

item.title: Fukui Tanabata Festival & Fireworks: A Summer Star Festival Celebration — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Tanabata Festival is part of the nationwide summer Tanabata (Star Festival) tradition, which celebrates the legend of two star-crossed lovers allowed to meet just once a year, and fills the city with colourful paper streamer decorations and bamboo branches hung with handwritten wishes. Fukui’s celebration typically combines these festive decorations with food stalls and, on the main evening, a fireworks display, making it a lively seasonal event drawing residents and visitors together for a summer night out.

item.title: Kusatsu Winter Illumination & Fireworks: A Steaming Yubatake After Dark — Guide
item.description: Kusatsu Onsen takes on a magical atmosphere each winter as coloured lights illuminate the steaming Yubatake and surrounding streets, the rising vapour catching the light in an ethereal display against the cold night air. Some winter evenings feature fireworks displays over the town, adding to the festive atmosphere, while visitors wander between illuminated streets, warm public foot baths, and steaming restaurants serving hot regional dishes suited to the season. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kusatsu, Gunma Hours Evening illumination, roughly December–February Admission Free to view Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Weekday evenings for smaller crowds; check for specific fireworks dates What to See The steaming Yubatake illuminated with coloured lights.

item.title: Mihama Fireworks Festival: A Summer Fireworks Display Over Wakasa Bay — Guide
item.description: The Mihama Fireworks Festival is held each summer along the scenic Wakasa Bay coast in southern Fukui, lighting up the night sky over the water in one of the region’s most anticipated seasonal events. The setting over the bay allows the fireworks to reflect across the water’s surface, and the beachside location draws crowds who gather along the coast to watch the display, often combined with food stalls and a festive summer evening atmosphere in the surrounding area.

item.title: Niigata Matsuri: The Port City's Grand Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: Niigata Matsuri is the city’s largest annual festival, held each August and combining several older local celebrations into a single grand event that fills the streets around the Shinano River with parades, traditional dance performances and food stalls over several days. The festival culminates in a large-scale fireworks display over the river, drawing enormous crowds to the waterfront, and its energetic street parades feature elaborately decorated floats and thousands of participating dancers.

item.title: Chichibu Night Festival: One of Japan's Three Great Float Festivals — Guide
item.description: The Chichibu Night Festival, held each December, is ranked among Japan’s three great float festivals and designated a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. Six enormous, elaborately decorated floats — some weighing several tonnes and adorned with intricate wood carvings, lanterns and tapestries — are hauled through the streets by teams of local residents, accompanied by traditional flute and drum music, while a spectacular fireworks display lights the winter sky above. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Chichibu, Saitama Hours Evening, December 2–3 each year Admission Free to view Time needed 3–5 hours (evening parade + fireworks) Best time December 3 evening (main event) What to See Six enormous decorated floats, some weighing several tonnes.

item.title: Kisarazu Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi & Access
item.description: Each summer, the bayside city of Kisarazu lights up the night with one of inner Tokyo Bay’s biggest fireworks festivals (hanabi) — a beloved August tradition that sends tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water. Held along the Kisarazu waterfront near the foot of the Aqua-Line, the display reflects spectacularly off the bay and draws huge crowds in summer yukata to picnic, snack at festival stalls and watch the sky erupt in colour.

item.title: Tenjin Matsuri Guide: Osaka's Great River & Fire Festival
item.description: Held every July, Tenjin Matsuri is one of Japan’s three great festivals (with Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri and Tokyo’s Kanda Matsuri) and the biggest party in Osaka. Over a thousand years old, it honours Sugawara no Michizane, the deity of learning, enshrined at Osaka Tenmangu. The festival builds to a spectacular evening climax on July 25: a grand boat procession (funa-togyo) of around a hundred lantern-lit vessels gliding up and down the Okawa River, accompanied by drums, traditional music, and a fireworks finale reflected in the water.

item.title: Yokohama Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi, Spots & Access
item.description: There are few sights more magical than fireworks (hanabi) bursting over Yokohama’s Minato Mirai skyline, their colours mirrored in the bay beside the glowing Ferris wheel and illuminated towers. Summer is firework season across Japan, and Yokohama’s waterfront — with its open harbour, parks and promenades — makes one of the country’s most photogenic backdrops. From large bay-side festivals to special event displays, tens of thousands gather on warm evenings in yukata to watch the sky light up.

item.title: Hiroshima Events 2026: Peace Ceremony, Flower Festival, Kangensai & Fireworks
item.description: Hiroshima’s event calendar is unusually wide in tone. The August 6 Peace Memorial Ceremony is one of the world’s most significant annual commemorations; the Kangensai boat festival on Miyajima is one of Japan’s oldest and most atmospheric Shinto rituals; the Flower Festival draws over a million people during Golden Week. Add summer fireworks over the bay, a legendary sake festival, and a beloved baseball team, and Hiroshima rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Chiba Events 2026: Fireworks, Tokyo Game Show, Gion Festivals & Disney
item.description: Chiba is where most visitors land (Narita Airport) and where Tokyo Disney Resort actually sits — but the prefecture’s own 2026 event calendar is far richer than a transit stop suggests. It hosts some of the Kanto region’s biggest summer fireworks, two UNESCO-linked Gion float festivals on the same weekend, the world’s largest video-game show, a temple-steps display of thirty thousand hina dolls, and whale-and-dolphin watching off its Pacific coast. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Saitama Events 2026: Chichibu Night Festival, Kawagoe Matsuri & Fireworks
item.description: Just north of Tokyo, Saitama is an easy day trip that hides two of Japan’s most important festivals. The Chichibu Night Festival and the Kawagoe Matsuri are both UNESCO-recognised float processions, and the prefecture also stages a Guinness-record firework, a hillside of half a million moss-phlox blooms, and the “Little Edo” charm of Kawagoe’s warehouse district. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Hokkaido Events 2026: Snow Festival, Yosakoi Soran, Lavender & Fireworks
item.description: Hokkaido’s events follow its dramatic seasons. Winter brings the snow-and-ice spectacle the island is world-famous for — the Sapporo Snow Festival and a string of candle-lit and ice-carved events across the region. Then summer flips the script entirely: energetic street dancing in June, lavender fields and hillside fireworks in July, and one of Japan’s great food festivals in autumn. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Osaka Events 2026: Festivals, Fireworks, Sumo & USJ Happenings
item.description: Osaka does festivals the way it does everything — loud, warm, and food-first. The city’s 2026 calendar runs from one of Japan’s three great festivals (Tenjin Matsuri, with its river-boat procession and fireworks) to the heart-stopping cart races of Kishiwada Danjiri, a spring Grand Sumo tournament, the year’s biggest anime collaborations at Universal Studios Japan, and a cherry-blossom tunnel opened for just one week. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.
